title: Change a furnace filter
summary: Put a clean filter in a forced-air furnace, the right way round, so it runs as it should.
for: Anyone with a forced-air furnace. No experience needed; the furnace's own manual says where its filter is.

tools.note: Only if the filter door is screwed shut.

materials.note: A new filter the same size as the old one. Not needed if yours is a washable filter.

stop_and_call.do: Leave the building now, leaving doors and windows open behind you. Do not switch lights on or off, do not make a spark, and do not use a phone while you are inside. From a safe distance, away from the smell, call 911 and your gas company.
stop_and_call.who: Emergency services (911 in the United States) and your gas company

steps.text: Turn off the furnace's electrical supply.
why: The maker's instructions turn the electrical supply off before a filter door or the blower door comes off. Its general rule for any maintenance is to turn off the gas and the electrical supply.
detail: If you cannot tell how your furnace's power is turned off, ask whoever services it to show you (our reading). ENERGY STAR notes that a contractor can show you how to change the filter.

steps.text: Open the filter door or cover and slide the old filter out.
detail: Where the filter sits depends on how the furnace is built. One maker's manual shows three places: in the return-air duct, in a cabinet beside the furnace, and inside the blower compartment. Your furnace's manual says which yours has.

safety.short: Mind the sheet-metal edges: the maker's manual says to wear safety glasses and work gloves.

steps.text: Write down the size of the old filter.
why: A new filter goes in only if it is the same size: the maker's instructions replace a filter only with one of the same part number and size.

steps.text: Is the old filter one you throw away, or a washable one?
detail: Some furnaces come with permanent, washable filters; others take throw-away ones. The furnace's manual says which it takes.

steps.text: Take a new filter of the same size.
Wash the filter by spraying tap water through it from the side the air comes out of, rinse it, and let it dry.
detail: Spraying against the way the air flows pushes the dust back out the way it came in (our reading). Do not oil or coat it: the maker's instructions say that is neither recommended nor needed.

steps.text: Slide the filter into its slot with the arrow on its frame pointing toward the furnace.
why: The arrow shows the way air should flow through the filter: from the room, through the filter, into the furnace.

steps.text: Look again: does the arrow on the filter point toward the furnace?
Close the filter door or cover.

safety.short: Never run the furnace without a filter, or with its filter door off.
full: The maker's instructions warn that running the furnace without a filter, or with the filter's door removed, could cause a fire, an injury or a death.

steps.text: Turn the furnace's electrical supply back on.

worked_if: The filter door is closed and the furnace runs as it did before.
The arrow on the filter points toward the furnace.

problems.sign: The arrow on the filter points away from the furnace.
problems.why: The filter is in backwards: the arrow should point the way the air flows, toward the furnace.
problems.fix: Take the filter out, turn it round and slide it back in.

problems.sign: The filter door will not close.
problems.why: The filter may be the wrong size, or not all the way into its slot (our reading).
problems.fix: Take it out and compare its size with the old filter's. Do not run the furnace with the door off.
Replace it rather than washing it.

repeat.note: ENERGY STAR's advice: check the filter every month, especially in the heavy-use months of winter and summer; change it if it looks dirty after a month, and at a minimum every 3 months.

sources.title: Heat & Cool Efficiently
sources.quote: At a minimum, change the filter every 3 months.
sources.note: Also: check the filter every month, especially during heavy use months (winter and summer); change it if it looks dirty after a month; a dirty filter slows air flow and makes the system work harder.

sources.title: Maintenance Checklist
sources.quote: Your contractor can show you how to do this.
sources.note: Said of inspecting, cleaning or changing the air filters once a month.

sources.title: 58DXT, 58UXT WeatherMaker 8000 Two-Stage Induced-Combustion Gas Furnaces: Service and Maintenance Instructions, Catalog No. 535-80047
sources.quote: If the filter has an airflow direction arrow, the arrow must point toward the blower.
sources.note: One maker's manual for one family of gas furnaces, read as a downloaded PDF with its text extracted locally; dated by its copyright line. Its warnings: turn off gas and electrical supplies before any maintenance or service; wear safety glasses and work gloves; sharp metal edges can cause injury. Its owner steps: turn off the electrical supply before removing the filter cabinet door or the blower access door; filters in the return-air duct, a media cabinet or the blower compartment; permanent, washable filters cleaned by spraying tap water through them from the opposite direction of airflow, rinsed and let dry, oiling or coating not recommended or required; a disposable media filter replaced only with one of the same part number and size; replace if torn; and the warning, 'Never operate unit without a filter or with filter access door removed. A failure to follow this warning could result in fire, personal injury, or death.' Other furnaces follow their own manuals.

sources.title: New filter inserted in furnace filter slot on return side of furnace, arrow on side of filter frame pointing toward furnace (image caption)
sources.quote: pointing in the direction of airflow, which is toward the furnace
sources.note: A Building America Solution Center (US Department of Energy, by PNNL) image caption, not a guide. The page shows no date; the image's file name suggests August 2024.

sources.title: Gas Emergencies
sources.quote: Call 9-1-1 and your natural gas utility (if you know the number) from a safe distance, away from the odor.
sources.note: Also: if indoors, leave immediately; do not turn lights on or off; do not make calls from a landline or a cell phone while at home; do not cause a spark; wait for the gas company or emergency services to say it is safe to return. A Pennsylvania agency's page; 911 is the emergency number in the United States.
